Cautiously hawkish with a stronger credit headwind. The FOMC raised the policy rate to 4.75–5% and continued QT while emphasizing “cumulative tightening” and policy lags. It acknowledged that banking stresses will tighten credit and weigh on activity, hiring, and inflation, even as it underscored that the banking system is “sound and resilient.” Implementation details—higher interest on reserve balances, calibrated ON RRP and standing repo, and maintained runoff caps—reinforce rate control and liquidity backstops.

SLOOS overlay: Banks report broad-based tightening of lending standards and weaker demand across key categories—C&I loans and multiple CRE segments (nonfarm nonresidential, construction/land development, multifamily). Firms cite decreased financing needs for plant/equipment, M&A, inventories, and accounts receivable, and foreign banks also report weaker C&I demand. These findings imply a more pronounced contraction in credit availability and demand than a policy-read alone would suggest, amplifying the downside risks to growth and employment while likely easing inflation pressures over time.

Netting these, the communication remains restrictive but the SLOOS evidence shifts the balance more negatively versus a neutral baseline and relative to the prior assessment.
